title: Sources of Magnetic Field
summary: Currents create magnetic fields. A long straight wire produces $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; a loop's center gives $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$; a solenoid gives $B = \mu_0 n I$; and two parallel wires exert $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$ on each other. Ampère's law ties current to field. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$; Vol. 2, Ch. 12.)

Biot-Savart law.plain: A rule for the magnetic field a small piece of current creates.
Biot-Savart law.in_class: $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$ — the magnetic analog of Coulomb's law.

Ampère's law.plain: A shortcut for the magnetic field around symmetric current arrangements.
Ampère's law.in_class: $\oint \vec B \cdot d\vec l = \mu_0 I_{enc}$ — the magnetic version of Gauss's law.

permeability.plain: How easily a material or space supports a magnetic field.
permeability.in_class: $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ T·m/A for vacuum; appears in every field formula here.

solenoid.plain: A coil of wire that makes a nearly uniform field inside.
solenoid.in_class: $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $n$ is turns per meter.

toroid.plain: A solenoid bent into a doughnut ring.
toroid.in_class: Field is confined inside: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi r}$.

magnetic dipole.plain: A current loop that acts like a tiny bar magnet.
magnetic dipole.in_class: Has a magnetic moment $\mu = IA$; feels a torque in an external field.

field of a wire.plain: The circular magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire.
field of a wire.in_class: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$; direction from the right-hand rule.

concept_sections.heading: Moving charge makes a field
concept_sections.explanation: Just as a field pushes on current, current creates a field. Around a long straight wire the field circles the wire (right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl the way $B$ points) with magnitude $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, falling off as $1/r$.

concept_sections.heading: Loops and the Biot–Savart idea
concept_sections.explanation: Each little piece of current contributes a bit of field (the Biot–Savart law). Adding them around a circular loop of radius $R$ gives a field at the center $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$, pointing along the loop's axis. Loops concentrate field — the building block of electromagnets.

concept_sections.heading: Force between parallel wires
concept_sections.explanation: Each wire sits in the other's field, so they push or pull: $\dfrac{F}{L} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$. Currents in the same direction attract; opposite currents repel. This force once defined the ampere itself.

concept_sections.heading: The solenoid
concept_sections.explanation: A solenoid is a long coil of $n$ turns per meter. Inside, the fields of all the loops add to give a nearly uniform $B = \mu_0 n I$, while outside it is weak. Add an iron core and you have a strong, switchable electromagnet.

concept_sections.heading: Ampère's law
concept_sections.explanation: Ampère's law says the field summed around any closed loop equals $\mu_0$ times the current threading it: $\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enc}$. With symmetry it gives the wire and solenoid results quickly — the magnetic analog of Gauss's law.

real_world_examples.title: Electromagnet / solenoid
real_world_examples.scenario: A junkyard crane lifts cars with a coil, then drops them by switching off.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A solenoid's field $B = \mu_0 n I$ (boosted by an iron core) is strong while current flows and vanishes when it stops — controllable magnetism.

real_world_examples.title: MRI scanner
real_world_examples.scenario: An MRI uses an enormous, steady magnetic field.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Superconducting solenoid coils carry huge currents to make a uniform $B = \mu_0 n I$ of a few tesla across the patient.

real_world_examples.title: Power-line fields
real_world_examples.scenario: Compasses waver near heavy power cables.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The current creates a circling field $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$ that drops with distance — why fields fall off quickly as you step away.

problems.prompt: Find the magnetic field $0.050$ m from a long wire carrying $10$ A. (Use $\mu_0/2\pi = 2\times10^{-7}$.)
A solenoid has $n = 1000$ turns/m and carries $2.0$ A. Find the field inside. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$.)
Find the field at the center of a single circular loop of radius $0.10$ m carrying $5.0$ A.
Two parallel wires $0.020$ m apart each carry $10$ A. Find the force per length between them.
At what distance from a long wire carrying $5.0$ A is the field $1.0\times10^{-5}$ T?
A solenoid $0.50$ m long has $2000$ turns and carries $3.0$ A. Find the field inside.
problems.hint: First find $n = N/L$, then $B = \mu_0 n I$.

problems.prompt: Two parallel wires $0.10$ m apart carry $20$ A each in the same direction. Find the force per length and state attract or repel.
problems.hint: Same direction → attract; use $F/L = \mu_0 I_1I_2/(2\pi d)$.

problems.prompt: Two wires $0.10$ m apart carry $10$ A in opposite directions. Find the net field at the midpoint between them.
solution_steps: Each wire is $0.050$ m from the midpoint: $B = (2\times10^{-7})\dfrac{10}{0.050} = 4.0\times10^{-5}$ T.
Opposite currents make both fields point the same way at the midpoint, so they add.
problems.hint: Find each wire's field at the midpoint; for opposite currents they add there.
